day1.title: Day 1 — Get Started with Red Hat Enterprise Linux
day1.subtitle: An introduction to Linux, RHEL, the command line, and file management fundamentals.

items: Explain the purpose of open source, Linux, Linux distributions, and Red Hat Enterprise Linux.
Log in to a Linux system and run simple commands from the shell.
Describe how Linux organizes files and manage them from the command line.

blocks.html: Linux traces its lineage back to the UNIX operating system, developed through decades of incremental innovation:

items: 1969 — Thompson and Ritchie create AT&T UNIX.
1972 — UNIX version 2 is rewritten in C.
1977 — BSD (Berkeley Software Distribution) is released.
1983 — Richard Stallman launches the GNU Project.
1987 — Andy Tannenbaum creates Minix.
1991 — Linus Torvalds creates i386 Linux.
1992 — Linux is licensed under the GPL (GNU General Public License).

blocks.html: Key Takeaway: Linux emerged from decades of UNIX development, combining Torvalds' kernel with the GNU Project's tools and the GPL's open licensing model.

A Linux distribution (distro) packages the Linux kernel together with system tools, libraries, and software into a complete, installable operating system. Distributions descend from UNIX-inspired lineages and split into distinct families:

items: Debian family → Ubuntu → Linux Mint
Fedora family → RHEL → CentOS, Oracle Linux
SUSE family → SLES → OpenSUSE
Other distributions include Red Hat Linux, Fedora, and Kali Linux

blocks.html: All distributions share the same Linux kernel at their core, but differ in package management, target use case, and support model.
Linux's popularity across servers, desktops, and embedded systems comes from a combination of practical advantages:

items: Open Source — source code is freely available and modifiable.
It is Free — no licensing cost for most distributions.
High Security — a strong permissions model and active security community.
High Stability — long uptimes and reliable performance.
Ease of Maintenance — centralized package management and scripting support.
Runs on Any Hardware — from embedded devices to enterprise servers.
Customization — deep configurability at every layer.
Community Support — a large global base of contributors and users.
Education and Support — extensive documentation and learning resources.

blocks.html: Quick check: Run uname -a and cat /etc/os-release to confirm your distro family — Debian shows ID=ubuntu, RHEL shows ID=rhel.

blocks.code:
uname -r
cat /etc/os-release | grep -E "^(NAME|VERSION|ID)"
lsb_release -a 2>/dev/null || echo "lsb_release not installed"

blocks.html: Linux systems are built from three core layers, each with a distinct role.
The kernel is the core of the operating system.

items: Contains components such as device drivers.
Loads into RAM when the machine boots.
Stays resident in RAM until the machine powers off.

blocks.html: The shell is the interface through which a user communicates with the kernel.

items: Common shells include C shell, ksh, and Bash.
Bash is the most commonly used shell on Linux.
The shell parses commands entered by the user and translates them into logical segments executed by the kernel or other utilities.

blocks.html: Key Takeaway: The kernel manages hardware and system resources, while the shell provides the interface users rely on to issue commands to that kernel.
Mental model: CLI → Shell (bash) → Kernel → Hardware. Verify your shell with echo $SHELL and kernel with uname -r.

items: Creating a VM: File -> New VM -> Installing Redhat on VMware (Recommended: 2 processors, 2 cores).
Network Types: Bridged, NAT, Host-only (chosen according to the IP range).
Choose NAT when setting up VMware.
Redhat Developer Account: You can use developer account credentials to log in to a Redhat server with a GUI on VMware.

blocks.html: There are two primary ways to reach a Linux shell:

items: From a Graphical User Interface (GUI) — opening a terminal application within a desktop environment such as GNOME.
Remote access over Secure Shell (SSH) — connecting to the system from another machine.

blocks.html: Commands in Linux follow a consistent syntax:

items: Each item is separated by a space.
Options modify the command's behavior.
Arguments are file names or other information the command needs.
Multiple commands can be separated with a semicolon (;).

blocks.html: Spacing matters. Options must be separated from the command and from each other correctly.
Important: Options must be attached directly to their dash (no space between - and the letter), and the order of arguments relative to options matters for correct parsing.
Bash provides keyboard shortcuts that save time when editing commands at the prompt:

head: Shortcut
Action
rows: Jump to the beginning of the command line.
Jump to the end of the command line.
Clear from the cursor to the beginning of the command line.
Clear from the cursor to the end of the command line.
Jump to the beginning of the previous word on the command line.
Jump to the end of the next word on the command line.
Search the history list of commands for a pattern.

blocks.html: Spacing trap: ls - l (space) ≠ ls -l. The shell splits on spaces — - must hug its letter. Also mail test root -s fails because -s must precede the address.

whoami; pwd; echo $HOME
ls -l /dev | head

sections.title: Manage Files from the Command Line

blocks.html: Linux organizes all data in a single hierarchical tree of files and directories, rooted at /.
Every directory branches from the single root (/), and each serves a specific, standardized purpose.

head: Location
Purpose
rows: Installed software, shared libraries, include files, and read-only program data.
Configuration files specific to this system.
Variable data that persists between boots — databases, cache directories, log files, printer-spooled documents, and website content.

Runtime data for processes started since the last boot, including process ID and lock files. Contents are recreated on reboot; this directory consolidates /var/run and /var/lock from earlier RHEL versions.
Personal data and configuration files for regular users.
Home directory for the administrative superuser, root.
World-writable space for temporary files. Files untouched for 10 days are deleted automatically.
Files needed to start the boot process.
Special *device files* used by the system to access hardware.

blocks.html: Note: A second temporary directory, /var/tmp, also exists — files there are deleted automatically only after 30 days of inactivity, giving them a longer lifespan than files in /tmp.
Every file in Linux has a type, indicated by a leading symbol in a long directory listing (ls -l):

Should:
- Be descriptive.
- Use only alphanumeric characters: uppercase, lowercase, numbers, @, _.

Should Not:
- Include embedded blanks (spaces).
- Contain shell metacharacters: * ? > < / ; & ! [ ] | \ ' " ( ) { }

Additional rules:
- Filenames are case sensitive.
- Filenames starting with a . are hidden.
- Maximum filename length is 255 characters.
Every file and directory can be referenced two ways:

items: Absolute path — the full path starting from the root /, unambiguous regardless of the current location (e.g., /home/alice/document.txt or /var/log/messages).
Relative path — a path expressed relative to the current working directory, which changes depending on where you currently are in the file system.

blocks.html: Key Takeaway: An absolute path always starts at / and works from anywhere; a relative path is shorter but only valid from your current location.
Spaces & dashes: Quote names with spaces: touch "my notes.txt" or escape touch my\ notes.txt. For leading dash: touch -- -weird and rm -- -weird — -- ends option parsing.

blocks.code:
touch "my file.txt" && ls -b
touch -- -dash && ls -l -- -dash
rm -- -dash
mkdir -p "My Projects/src" && tree -L 2 2>/dev/null || find . -maxdepth 2 | sort

sections.title: Inodes, Hard Links, and Soft Links

blocks.html: Linux allocates an index node (inode) for every file and directory in the filesystem. Inodes do not store the actual file data — instead, they store the metadata that points to where the file's data blocks live on disk.

items: File type
Permissions
Hard links count
Owner ID
Group ID
Soft/Hard Links
Access Control List (ACLs)
Size of file
Timestamp (access time)
Timestamp (modification time)

blocks.html: A hard link is a direct reference to a file's inode, while a file itself is also just a name pointing to an inode. A soft link does not reference the inode directly — it points to the file name/path instead, and both hard links and soft links are maintained by the file system.

head: Soft Link
Hard Link
rows: An alias to the original file, similar to the shortcut feature in Windows OS.
The exact replica of the original file it is pointing to.
Contains only the location to the original file, not the actual data.
Contains the actual content of the file.
Has a different inode value pointing to the original value.
Shares the same inode value pointing to the same file location.
Cannot be created outside the filesystem.
Becomes inaccessible when the original file is removed.
Changes in the hard-linked file will reflect in the other files.
Can link both to a file or a directory.
Can only link to a file, not a directory.

blocks.html: Key Takeaway: A hard link is another name for the exact same file data, while a soft link is a pointer to a file's location that breaks if the original is deleted.
See it live: ls -i file; stat file; df -i — if df -i shows 100% IUse, you can be “out of space” even with free GB.

blocks.code:
echo hello > a.txt
ln a.txt hard.txt
ln -s a.txt soft.txt
ls -li a.txt hard.txt soft.txt
cat soft.txt
echo world >> a.txt
cat hard.txt # shows world too (same inode)
cat soft.txt

blocks.html: Bash supports pattern matching (globbing) to efficiently reference multiple files at once.

head: Pattern
Matches
rows: Any string of zero or more characters.
Any one character in the enclosed class (between the square brackets).
Any one character *not* in the enclosed class.
Any one character *not* in the enclosed class.
Any printable character not a space or alphanumeric.
Any single white space character. This may include tabs, newlines, carriage returns, form feeds, or spaces.

blocks.html: Regular expressions (regex) extend pattern matching with more powerful syntax, commonly used with tools like grep and sed:

head: Symbol
Description
rows: Matches zero or more times the preceding character.

blocks.html: Key Takeaway: Shell pattern matching (globbing) and regular expressions are related but distinct — globbing operates on filenames at the shell level, while regex is a more expressive matching language used inside text-processing tools.
Glob vs regex: Shell glob *.txt is not regex .*\.txt. Globs expand before the command runs — try echo *.txt to see.

blocks.code:
touch a.txt B.TXT file1.log
ls *.txt        # glob
ls [a-z]*.txt    # range
ls [!a]*        # not a
# regex with grep (different!)
grep -E "^a.*\.txt$" <(ls -1)
# speed: fixed strings
 grep -F "error" /var/log/syslog 2>/dev/null | head

items: Linux is an open-source operating system descended from UNIX, licensed under the GPL, with distributions (distros) built around a shared kernel but differing in packaging and tooling.
The kernel manages hardware and resources; the shell (commonly Bash) is the interface for issuing commands.
Commands follow the syntax command [options] [arguments], and correct spacing between options is essential.
Linux organizes everything into a single hierarchical filesystem rooted at /, with standardized directories like /etc, /var, /home, and /tmp serving specific purposes.
Every file and directory has an inode storing its metadata; hard links share an inode with the original file, while soft links merely point to its path.
Bash pattern matching and regular expressions allow efficient, flexible operations across many files at once.

sections.title: Get Help in Red Hat Enterprise Linux

blocks.html: Linux systems ship with an extensive built-in reference: the manual pages (man pages). Knowing how to navigate them turns any unfamiliar command into a solvable problem.
The manual is divided into numbered sections, each covering a different category of documentation:

head: Section
Content Type
rows: User commands (both executable and shell programs)
System calls (kernel routines invoked from user space)
File formats (for many configuration files and structures)
Conventions, standards, and miscellaneous (protocols, file systems)
System administration and privileged commands (maintenance tasks)

blocks.html: Each man page follows a consistent internal structure, making it easy to jump straight to the information you need:

head: Heading
Description
rows: Subject name — usually a command or file name — with a very brief description.
In-depth description to provide a basic understanding of the topic.
Explanation of the command execution options.
Examples of how to use the command, function, or file.
A list of files and directories related to the man page.
Related information, normally other man page topics.
Information about who has contributed to the development of the topic.

blocks.html: Key Takeaway: Manual pages are organized by section and follow a predictable internal layout, so once you know the structure, finding the right information becomes fast and consistent.
When stuck: man -k "copy file" (apropos) finds commands by description. If empty, run sudo mandb once to build the index.

blocks.code:
whatis passwd
man -k "print files"
man 1 passwd | head -n 20
man 5 passwd | head -n 20
passwd --help 2>&1 | head

sections.title: Create, View, and Edit Text Files

blocks.html: Working efficiently at the command line means controlling where output goes and how commands connect to each other.
Every running program or command has three standard communication channels, each identified by a file descriptor (FD) number:

items: Standard Input (stdin) — FD 0, typically the keyboard.
Standard Output (stdout) — FD 1, typically the screen.
Standard Error (stderr) — FD 2, typically the screen, but separately from stdout.

blocks.html: These channels can be redirected to files instead of the terminal, letting you save output, discard errors, or feed input from a file.
A pipeline connects the standard output (stdout) of one process directly to the standard input (stdin) of another, allowing commands to be chained together to process data in stages.

head: Operator
Behavior
rows: Discard stderr error messages by redirecting them to /dev/null.
Redirect stdout and stderr to overwrite the same file.
Redirect stdout and stderr to append to the same file.

blocks.html: This redirects both stdout and stderr into output.log, overwriting any existing content.
vim is a modal command-line text editor — its behavior changes depending on which mode you're in.

items: Command mode — the default mode for navigation and issuing editing commands.
Insert mode — entered with i or a, used for typing text directly; return to command mode with Esc.
Visual mode — entered with v, V, or Ctrl+V, used for selecting text.
Extended command mode (Ex mode) — entered with :, used for saving, quitting, and advanced operations.

head: Command
Action
rows: Save and quit the current file.
Save the current file if there are unsaved changes, then quit.
Save the current file and remain in editor.
Quit the current file (only if there are no unsaved changes).
Quit the current file, ignoring any unsaved changes.

blocks.html: Quick reference for moving between modes and performing common editing actions:

items: To edit mode: I, i, a, A (variants of insert, positioned at line start, cursor, after cursor, or line end).
Cut, copy, paste line: dd (cut/delete line), yy (yank/copy line), p (paste).
Delete char/word: x, X, dw.
Join lines: J.
Search, repeat: / (search), n (repeat search).
Cursor movement: h (left), j (down), k (up), l (right), 1G (go to first line), G (go to last line), $ (end of line).
Undo, redo: u (undo), . (repeat last change).
Save & exit: ZZ.
Ex mode: : — includes search and replace (:%s /old/new/g), change settings (:set ...), and save/exit commands (:w, :w!, :q, :q!, :wq, :x).
From Edit mode, or returns to Command mode.

blocks.html: Key Takeaway: vim's power comes from its distinct modes — navigate and issue commands in Command mode, type freely in Insert mode, and save/quit/search through Ex mode.
Linux shells support two categories of variables that control behavior and store data:

items: User-defined variables — created and set by the user for their own use in scripts or commands.
Shell variables — variables used or set by the shell itself to control its behavior and environment.

blocks.html: Redirection order matters: cmd > file 2>&1 works, but cmd 2>&1 > file does NOT — stderr goes to old stdout (screen). Use &> file as shorthand or > file 2>&1 at the end.

blocks.code:
echo hello > /tmp/demo.txt
cat /tmp/demo.txt
echo world >> /tmp/demo.txt
cat /tmp/demo.txt
# mix stdout+stderr
ls /tmp/nope /tmp/demo.txt > /tmp/out.txt 2>&1; cat /tmp/out.txt
ls /tmp/nope /tmp/demo.txt &> /tmp/both.txt; cat /tmp/both.txt
# pipes + status
echo "a b c" | tr " " "\n" | sort | uniq -c
echo ${PIPESTATUS[@]} # shows each pipe exit code

blocks.html: wc stands for word count, and despite the name, it actually counts three things at once: lines, words, and characters.
Here, echo "nti aiops" simply prints the text nti aiops, and that text is piped into wc, which analyzes it. The output has three numbers, always in this order:

items: 1 line — because echo only produced one line of text
2 words — "nti" and "aiops" are two separate words
10 characters — counting every letter and the space between them

blocks.html: Often you don't need all three — just one specific count. You can add a flag to wc to isolate exactly what you want:
This returns only the word count (2), with nothing else cluttering the output.

items: ls -R /etc lists everything inside /etc, and the -R flag makes it recursive — meaning it doesn't just list the top-level folder, it digs into every subfolder inside it too, listing everything at every depth
Piping that into wc -l counts how many total lines were produced — effectively telling you how many files and folders exist inside /etc and all its subfolders combined

blocks.html: This shows how small commands combine into powerful one-liners: instead of manually counting hundreds of files, one line does it instantly.
A user account provides security boundaries between different people and programs that can run commands. The system distinguishes user accounts by a unique identification number, the user ID (UID).
There are three main types of user accounts:

items: Superuser — the administrative account with full system privileges.
System users — accounts used internally by system processes.
Regular users — accounts for people who log in interactively.

blocks.html: UID ranges follow a standard convention on Red Hat systems:

items: UID 0 — always assigned to the superuser account, root.
UID 1–200 — a range of "system users" assigned statically to system processes by Red Hat.

UID 201–999 — a range of "system users" used by system processes that do not own files on the file system; typically assigned dynamically from the available pool when the software needing them is installed.
UID 1000+ — the range available for assignment to regular users.

blocks.html: User account information is stored in /etc/passwd, with each line following a fixed colon-separated format:

items: Username for this user (user01).
Password placeholder — the encrypted password used to be stored here, but has moved to /etc/shadow. This field should always be x.
UID number for this user account (1000).
GID number for this user account's primary group (1000).
Real name for this user (User One).
Home directory for this user (/home/user01) — the initial working directory when the shell starts, containing the user's data and configuration settings.

Default shell program for this user, which runs on login (/bin/bash). For a regular user, this is normally the program providing the command-line prompt; a system user might use /sbin/nologin if interactive logins are not allowed.

blocks.html: Group information is stored in /etc/group, also using a fixed colon-separated format:

items: Group name for this group (group01).
Obsolete group password field — should always be x.
GID number for this group (10000).
Member list — users who are members of this group as a supplementary group (user01, user02, user03).
When a new regular user is created, a new group with the same name as that user is created.
That group becomes the primary group for the new user, and the user is the only member of this User Private Group.
Users may also belong to supplementary groups.
Membership in supplementary groups is determined by the /etc/group file.
Users are granted access to files based on whether any of their groups — primary or supplementary — have access.

blocks.html: Key Takeaway: A user's file access is the union of permissions granted to their primary group and every supplementary group they belong to.
Two commands grant superuser privilege, with different models of access:

items: su — switches the current session directly to another user account (typically root), usually requiring that account's password.
sudo — allows a permitted user to run a single command with superuser privileges, typically using their own password, without fully switching accounts.

blocks.html: Password security information is stored separately in /etc/shadow, using this field structure:

items: Login name
Encrypted password
Days since Jan 1, 1970 that the password was last changed
Minimum days before the password may be changed
Maximum days after which the password must be changed
Days before expiration that the user is warned
Days after expiration that the account is disabled
Account expiration date, represented as the number of days since 1970-01-01
Blank field, reserved for future use

blocks.html: The chage command manages password aging policy per user, controlling the timeline between password changes, warnings, and account deactivation:

items: -d — sets the last change date.
-m — sets minimum days between changes.
-M — sets maximum days before a change is required.
-W — sets the number of warning days before expiration.
-I — sets the number of inactive days after expiration before the account is disabled.

blocks.html: This sets user03's password policy so it can be changed at any time (-m 0), must be changed at least every 90 days (-M 90), warns the user 7 days before expiration (-W 7), and disables the account after 14 days of inactivity past expiration (-I 14).
Key Takeaway: Password aging policy is enforced through /etc/shadow fields and configured with chage, giving administrators fine-grained control over how often users must update their credentials.
Shadow perms: /etc/shadow should be 640 and owned root:shadow — never chmod 777 /etc/shadow. Check with ls -l /etc/shadow; stat -c %a /etc/shadow.

blocks.code:
id
whoami; groups
sudo useradd -m demo1 2>&1 | head
sudo passwd demo1 # set, then
chage -l demo1
# lock vs disable
sudo passwd -l demo1  # locks password with !
sudo usermod -L demo1 # alternative
sudo userdel -r demo1 2>/dev/null; echo cleaned
# safe sudoers check
sudo visudo -c && echo "sudoers OK"
sudo grep -vE '^[[:space:]]*(#|$)' /etc/sudoers | head

items: Manual pages are organized into numbered sections and follow a predictable structure, making the man command a reliable first stop for troubleshooting.
Shell redirection and pipes let commands read from and write to files or each other, using standard input, output, and error streams.
vim is a modal editor — mastering the transitions between Command, Insert, Visual, and Ex modes is the key to using it efficiently.
User and group information lives in /etc/passwd and /etc/group, while sensitive password data and aging policy live in /etc/shadow.
Every regular user gets a private primary group at creation, and file access is determined by the combination of primary and supplementary group memberships.
su switches users entirely, while sudo grants privileged access to individual commands — both provide paths to superuser privilege with different security trade-offs.

blocks.html: This switches you to being the user omar. The dash (-) is crucial: it tells Linux to also load omar's entire environment, exactly as if omar had logged in directly himself — his home directory becomes your working directory, his shell configuration and variables load, his PATH becomes active. It will also display when omar last logged in, similar to what you'd see on a real login screen.

This still switches you to being omar, but it's a lighter switch — you keep your own current environment and variables rather than fully adopting his, and you typically remain in whatever directory you were already in rather than jumping to his home folder.

head: Behavior
su - username
su username
rows: Full environment, exactly as if that user logged in directly
Keeps your own current environment and variables
Jumps to that user's home directory
Typically remains in whatever directory you were already in
Shown, similar to a real login screen
Not part of this lighter switch
A true, full simulation of that user logging in (the safer, more predictable choice)
A quick, temporary permission switch without changing your whole environment

blocks.html: Every time someone runs a command with sudo, Linux checks a specific configuration file — /etc/sudoers — to decide whether that user is allowed to do that, and what exactly they're permitted to run (sometimes limited to specific commands, sometimes full access).
Why not just edit it with vim directly?

You technically could open /etc/sudoers with vim /etc/sudoers, but this is considered dangerous, because a single typo in this file could silently break the entire permissions system — potentially locking every single administrator out of sudo access at once, with no easy way back in.

Editing /etc/sudoers directly with a regular editor is dangerous — a single typo can silently break the entire permissions system, potentially locking every administrator out of sudo access at once, with no easy way back in.

visudo solves this by opening the file in a protected editing session that automatically checks your syntax for errors the moment you try to save. If it detects a mistake, it stops you, shows a warning, and refuses to save the broken version — giving you the chance to fix it or discard your changes safely. This built-in safety check is the entire reason visudo exists as a dedicated command instead of people just using a regular text editor.

sections.title: Man Pages — Getting Help in Linux

blocks.html: Every command in Linux comes bundled with its own official documentation, built right into the operating system. This is called a "man page" (short for manual page). Unlike searching the internet, man pages are always installed locally, always match the exact version of the command on your system, and work even if you have no internet connection — which matters a lot for servers.
Some words in Linux mean more than one thing. For example, passwd refers to:

items: A command you run to change a password
A file (/etc/passwd) that stores account information

blocks.html: If Linux just had one manual page per word, this would be confusing. So man pages are split into sections, each numbered:

head: Section
What it documents
Example
rows: File formats and configuration file structure

blocks.html: When you type man passwd without specifying a number, Linux shows you the lowest-numbered match it finds — usually the command page (section 1). If you specifically want the file-format explanation, you must ask for it directly with man 5 passwd.

This folder contains subdirectories like man1, man5, man8, etc. — one folder per section — each holding the actual manual files. You'll rarely need to browse here manually, but it's good to know this isn't magic; it's just organized text files on disk.

This tells you whether the command actually exists on this machine and where its files are stored (its binary program, its man page, and sometimes source files). This is useful troubleshooting before assuming "maybe this command isn't installed."
Man pages open using a "pager" program (usually called less), which lets you scroll through long text comfortably. Once inside, these keys help you move around:

head: Key
What it does
rows: Searches forward through the page for "word"
Jumps to the next occurrence of your last search
Jumps straight to the end of the document

blocks.html: This matters because man pages can be extremely long (some run hundreds of lines), so scrolling manually line-by-line would waste a lot of time.
whatis — gives you a one-line description instead of opening the whole manual:
Output is something short like: "passwd - update user's authentication tokens" — enough to jog your memory without committing to reading a full page.
man -k — lets you search by topic instead of by exact command name:

This searches through the short description line of every man page installed on the system and shows you every command whose description matches your keyword. This is incredibly useful when you know what you want to accomplish but don't remember the exact command name for it.
Behind the scenes, man -k relies on a search database called mandb. If man -k returns nothing on a fresh system, an administrator may need to run mandb once to build that index.
--help — nearly every Linux command supports this flag:
This prints a condensed list of all available options for that command directly in your terminal — much faster than opening the full man page when you just need a quick reminder of what flags exist.

blocks.html: Every command you run in Linux is silently connected to three data channels:

items: Input — where the command reads data from (by default, your keyboard)
Output — where the command sends its normal results (by default, your screen)
Error — where the command sends error/warning messages (by default, also your screen)

blocks.html: Linux internally labels these with numbers called File Descriptors (FDs):

head: Stream name
Purpose
File Descriptor number
rows: Where the command reads input from

blocks.html: Redirection means telling Linux "instead of the default location, send this stream somewhere else — usually into a file." This is one of the most powerful ideas in the Linux command line because it lets you automate things without ever touching a mouse or GUI.
This runs ls -l (list files with details) and instead of showing the results on your screen, sends them into a file called list.txt.

If list.txt already exists and has content, > will completely erase that content first, then write the new output. There's no confirmation prompt — it just happens. This is called overwriting, and it's the #1 way beginners accidentally lose data, so always double-check the filename before using a single >.

This runs date (which prints today's date and time) and adds that output to the end of list.txt, without touching or deleting whatever was already inside the file. Think of > as "replace the file" and >> as "add onto the file." This is exactly what you'd use to build up a running log over time — for example, appending a timestamp to a log file every time a script runs.

So far we've talked about output — but you can redirect input too. Normally, a command like sort waits for you to type names one by one on the keyboard. Instead, you can tell it to read directly from a file:

This makes sort read all the lines already stored in names.txt and immediately sort them alphabetically, without you needing to type anything interactively. This is less common day-to-day than output redirection, but it's important conceptually: input, output, and error are three separate, independently redirectable channels.
Because errors have their own File Descriptor (2), you can redirect only the errors, leaving normal output untouched:

items: find / -name passwd searches the entire filesystem (starting from /, the root) for anything named passwd

Because this search touches nearly every folder on the system, it will try to peek into directories you don't have permission to access — and each of those attempts generates a "Permission denied" error
2> grabs only those error messages (Channel 2) and sends them into /dev/null
/dev/null is a special file built into Linux that acts like a black hole — anything written into it is instantly discarded and gone forever. It's the standard way to "throw away" unwanted output.
Meanwhile, the actual successful search results (the file paths it did find) are not affected — they still print normally to your screen, because you only redirected Channel 2, not Channel 1

blocks.html: This pattern (2> /dev/null) is extremely common in real system administration to keep your terminal clean while running system-wide searches.
Sometimes you want both the normal results and the error messages saved — either together in one file, or split into two separate files.
Successful matches go into results.txt; error messages go into errors.txt.
&> — the modern shorthand for combining both into ONE file:
This single symbol tells Linux "send both the normal output AND the errors into this same file." It's a shortcut that saves you from writing two separate redirections.
2>&1 — the traditional (older, more explicit) method for combining streams:

This reads as: "send normal output (Channel 1) into all_output.txt, THEN also redirect errors (Channel 2) into wherever Channel 1 is currently pointing." The order matters here — 2>&1 must come after the > redirection, and it must be placed at the end of the command, because Linux processes these redirections left to right, and Channel 2 needs to know where Channel 1 is already pointing before it can copy that destination.

A pipeline is similar to redirection, but instead of sending a command's output into a file, it sends that output directly into another command as that command's input — with no file ever being created in between. The symbol used is the vertical bar |, called a "pipe."
Let's break this down step by step:

items: ls -l runs first, producing a detailed list of files and folders, where each line starts with a permission code like drwxr-xr-x (directories) or -rw-r--r-- (regular files)
The | takes that entire output and feeds it directly into the next command, grep, as if you had typed it in yourself

grep ^- searches through those lines and keeps only the ones that start with a dash - — because in ls -l output, a leading d means directory, a leading l means symbolic link, and a leading - specifically means "this is a regular file"

blocks.html: So the whole pipeline answers a specific question: "Show me only the actual files in this folder — skip the folders and shortcuts."

You can even chain multiple pipes together (cmd1 | cmd2 | cmd3), passing data through several filtering steps in sequence — this is one of Linux's most powerful features, letting you build complex operations out of small, simple tools.
wc stands for word count, and despite the name, it actually counts three things at once: lines, words, and characters.
Here, echo "nti aiops" simply prints the text nti aiops, and that text is piped into wc, which analyzes it. The output has three numbers, always in this order:

items: 1 line — because echo only produced one line of text
2 words — "nti" and "aiops" are two separate words
10 characters — counting every letter and the space between them

blocks.html: Often you don't need all three — just one specific count. You can add a flag to wc to isolate exactly what you want:
This returns only the word count (2), with nothing else cluttering the output.

items: ls -R /etc lists everything inside /etc, and the -R flag makes it recursive — meaning it doesn't just list the top-level folder, it digs into every subfolder inside it too, listing everything at every depth
Piping that into wc -l counts how many total lines were produced — effectively telling you how many files and folders exist inside /etc and all its subfolders combined

blocks.html: This shows how small commands combine into powerful one-liners: instead of manually counting hundreds of files, one line does it instantly.

sections.title: Vim / Vi — The Command-Line Text Editor

blocks.html: Most Linux servers don't have a graphical interface at all — no mouse, no windows, no Notepad-style app. So editing configuration files, scripts, or any text must happen entirely from the terminal. vim (an improved version of the older vi) is the most widely used tool for this.

blocks.html: A variable is simply a name that holds a piece of data, so you (or the system) can reuse that data later without retyping it. This concept exists in virtually every programming and scripting language, and Bash (the shell/command interpreter) is no exception.

Bash stands for "Bourne Again SHell," and it is the default shell used in Red Hat Enterprise Linux — meaning it's the actual program running behind the scenes that reads every command you type, interprets it, and executes it. When you open a "terminal," you're really talking directly to Bash.

items: Shell variables — these come built into Bash automatically and are used for configuration purposes. Examples include $PATH (a list of folders Bash searches through to find commands), $HOME (your home directory location), and $USER (your current username). You don't need to create these; they already exist the moment your shell starts.
User-defined variables — these are variables you create yourself to temporarily store any value you want during your session.

blocks.html: This creates a variable named x holding the value 5. Important: this variable is local to your current shell session only — if you open a new shell process from within this one (called a "sub-shell"), that sub-shell has no knowledge that x even exists.
export marks a variable so that it becomes visible to any sub-shell you open afterward, with the exact same name and value. Without export, a variable stays trapped in your current shell only.
Here's a way to test and truly understand this:

blocks.code:
x=5 # create a plain variable
bash # open a new sub-shell (a shell inside your shell)
echo $x # prints NOTHING — this sub-shell never inherited x
exit # leave the sub-shell, back to the original
export x=5 # create AND export in one step
bash # open a new sub-shell again
echo $x # prints 5 — this time it WAS inherited

blocks.html: This displays a full listing of every currently defined variable in your shell session — both the built-in shell variables and any custom ones you've created. It's typically a long list, useful mainly when troubleshooting or exploring what's already set.

Every user account on a Linux system — human or automated — has a unique numeric identifier called a UID (User ID). Linux uses this number internally to track ownership of files, processes, and permissions; usernames are really just human-friendly labels attached to these numbers.

1–200 (statically reserved by the OS itself, used for core system services) and 201–999 (dynamically assigned as software installs and creates its own service accounts)
These accounts exist to run background services/daemons — for example, the account that runs a web server or database process. They are not meant for humans to log into directly.
These are the normal, everyday human accounts — created by an administrator so real people can log in, have their own home folder, and do their own work

blocks.html: Understanding these ranges matters practically: if you ever list users on a system and see a UID under 1000, you immediately know "this is a service account, not a person" — which is important context when auditing security or troubleshooting.

The dash (-) is crucial: it tells Linux to also load omar's entire environment, exactly as if omar had logged in directly himself — his home directory becomes your working directory, his shell configuration and variables load, his PATH becomes active. It will also display when omar last logged in, similar to what you'd see on a real login screen.

This still switches you to being omar, but it's a lighter switch — you keep your own current environment and variables rather than fully adopting his, and you typically remain in whatever directory you were already in rather than jumping to his home folder.

blocks.html: Every time someone runs a command with sudo, Linux checks a specific configuration file — /etc/sudoers — to decide whether that user is allowed to do that, and what exactly they're permitted to run (sometimes limited to specific commands, sometimes full access).
Why not just edit it with vim directly?

You technically could open /etc/sudoers with vim /etc/sudoers, but this is considered dangerous, because a single typo in this file could silently break the entire permissions system — potentially locking every single administrator out of sudo access at once, with no easy way back in.

Editing /etc/sudoers directly with a regular editor is dangerous — a single typo can silently break the entire permissions system, potentially locking every administrator out of sudo access at once, with no easy way back in.

visudo solves this by opening the file in a protected editing session that automatically checks your syntax for errors the moment you try to save. If it detects a mistake, it stops you, shows a warning, and refuses to save the broken version — giving you the chance to fix it or discard your changes safely. This built-in safety check is the entire reason visudo exists as a dedicated command instead of people just using a regular text editor.

flashcards.q: What's the key difference between monolithic and microservices architecture when one service fails?
flashcards.a: In a monolithic architecture, if one service fails, all services go down. In microservices, if one service goes down, the rest of the services remain up.

flashcards.q: What role does a Load Balancer play, and what does RabbitMQ do?
flashcards.a: A Load Balancer balances traffic across services, while RabbitMQ acts as a queue for services.

flashcards.q: Why would you activate Swap (Virtual Memory), and give an example?
flashcards.a: To avoid system crashes — for example, activating Swap when uploading on AWS.

flashcards.q: What's the core difference between Linux and Unix in terms of source model?
flashcards.a: Linux is open source — customizable (including UI), no license, open to the public, and free (though some editions are licensed with nuances). Unix is closed source — private to its developers and not customizable.

flashcards.q: Who is the GPL (General Public License) associated with?
flashcards.a: Richard Stallman.

flashcards.q: What network type should you choose when setting up VMware, per these notes?
flashcards.a: NAT.

flashcards.q: What does `ifconfig` do, and is it needed on Ubuntu?
flashcards.a: It returns the IP address; this step can be skipped for Ubuntu.

flashcards.q: What is the correct way to combine CLI options, and which format is incorrect?
flashcards.a: `-l -d` and `-ld` are both correct ways to combine options; `-l d` is incorrect.

flashcards.q: What do `Ctrl+U` and `Ctrl+K` do in the terminal?
flashcards.a: `Ctrl+U` deletes the part of the command before the cursor; `Ctrl+K` deletes the part of the command after the cursor.

flashcards.q: What do `!500` and `!!` do in shell history?
flashcards.a: `!500` runs command number 500 from history; `!!` runs the last command in history.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `/bin` and `/sbin` per these notes?
flashcards.a: `/bin` is regular user data related ("shortcut"/"symbolic link"), while `/sbin` is super user data related ("shortcut"/"soft link").

flashcards.q: How often do `/tmp` and `/var/tmp` clear, and what do they have in common?
flashcards.a: `/tmp` clears every 10 days, and `/var/tmp` clears every 30 days; both are caches.

flashcards.q: What does `~` refer to in the shell prompt, for a regular user vs. root?
flashcards.a: `~` refers to the home directory — `/home/regularuser` for a regular user, and `/root` for the root user.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `cd -` and `cd ..`?
flashcards.a: `cd -` moves one step backwards to the previous directory; `cd ..` moves up one level in the directory tree (relative path).

flashcards.q: What does `ls -lthr` do?
flashcards.a: Produces a long-format, human-readable listing sorted by time, in reversed order.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `rm -r dir1` and `rm -fr dir1`?
flashcards.a: `rm -r dir1` removes a directory recursively but asks to verify first; `rm -fr dir1` removes it recursively without asking for confirmation.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `cat` and `less` for viewing file content?
flashcards.a: `cat` lists the full content of the file at once, while `less` is more organized and allows scrolling, using `Space` to move to the next page.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between a soft link and a hard link in terms of inode and size?
flashcards.a: A soft link has a different inode from the source and is just a pointer, so its size is unrelated to the original file's size. A hard link shares the same inode as the source, and its file size matches the source file's size.

flashcards.q: What does `ls -i` show?
flashcards.a: It displays the inode numbers of files.

flashcards.q: What does `grep -l Karim /etc/passwd` return if "Karim" is not found in the file?
flashcards.a: It returns nothing (no output), since `-l` only returns the file path when a match is found.

flashcards.q: What does the pattern `grep ^c..t$ /etc/passwd` match?
flashcards.a: Lines that start with 'c' and end with 't', with exactly 2 letters in between.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between an absolute path and a relative path?
flashcards.a: An absolute path is defined from the root directory `/` (e.g., `/usr/share/doc/`), while a relative path is defined relative to the current directory (e.g., `..`, `doc/`).

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `~` and `/home/`?
flashcards.a: `~` represents the home directory of the currently logged-in user (e.g., `/home/omar` or `/root`), while `/home/` is the base directory housing all individual user home folders.

flashcards.q: What does `cd -` do?
flashcards.a: Switches back to the previous working directory.

flashcards.q: How do you identify a directory, a regular file, and a symbolic link in `ls -l` output?
flashcards.a: `d` marks a directory, `-` marks a regular file, and `l` marks a symbolic link.

flashcards.q: What does `ls -li` show that plain `ls -l` doesn't?
flashcards.a: It additionally displays the inode numbers of the files.

flashcards.q: What does `mkdir -p dir1/dir2/dir3` do differently from plain `mkdir`?
flashcards.a: The `-p` (parent) flag creates the full nested directory structure recursively, creating any missing parent directories along the way.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `cp -r /etc/ /home/` and `cp -r /etc/* /home/`?
flashcards.a: `cp -r /etc/ /home/` copies the `/etc/` directory itself (with its contents) into `/home/`, while `cp -r /etc/* /home/` copies only the contents inside `/etc/` into `/home/`.

flashcards.q: What is the danger of running `rm -rf /`?
flashcards.a: It forcefully and recursively deletes the entire system, and this action is irreversible.

flashcards.q: What does `alias rm='rm -i'` do, and why does root use it by default?
flashcards.a: It makes `rm` prompt for confirmation before deleting each file. The root user defaults to this for safety, since root has permission to delete anything without restriction.

flashcards.q: What is an inode?
flashcards.a: An index node storing metadata about a file, such as file size, permissions, owner, timestamps, and block pointers, stored in the Inode Table.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between a hard link and a soft link if the source file is deleted?
flashcards.a: A hard link still works because it points to the same inode as the source file, so the data remains accessible. A soft link breaks because it only points to the target filename/path, producing an error when accessed.

flashcards.q: Can hard links be created for directories or across different filesystems?
flashcards.a: No — hard links cannot link directories and cannot be created across different filesystems/partitions. Soft links support both.

flashcards.q: What does `grep -v nologin /etc/passwd` do?
flashcards.a: Prints only the lines that do NOT contain "nologin" (inverted match).

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `grep -A 2` and `grep -B 2`?
flashcards.a: `-A 2` shows the matching line plus 2 lines after it; `-B 2` shows the matching line plus 2 lines before it.

flashcards.q: What does `grep -w shut /etc/passwd` match that plain `grep shut` would not?
flashcards.a: It matches only the whole word `shut`, not `shut` as a substring inside a longer word.

flashcards.q: What does `grep -e omar -e root /etc/passwd` do?
flashcards.a: Searches for multiple patterns simultaneously — lines containing `omar` OR `root`.

flashcards.q: What does the regex `grep '^c[aou]t$' /usr/share/dict/words` match?
flashcards.a: Exact 3-letter words starting with `c`, followed by `a`, `o`, or `u`, and ending with `t` — e.g. `cat`, `cot`, `cut`.

flashcards.q: What does `cut -d : -f 1,7 /etc/passwd` extract?
flashcards.a: Using `:` as the delimiter, it extracts fields 1 and 7 from each line — the username and the login shell.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `cut -c 1-5` and `cut -c 5-`?
flashcards.a: `cut -c 1-5` extracts characters from position 1 to 5, while `cut -c 5-` extracts characters from position 5 to the end of the line.

flashcards.q: What are the three checked advantages of Linux over Windows in this sheet?
flashcards.a: Security, Stability, and Maintenance (Linux also runs on different hardware, is free & open source, easy to customize, has community support, and offers a different UI experience).

flashcards.q: What are the roles of the Kernel and the Shell in Linux architecture?
flashcards.a: The Kernel works directly with the hardware, while the Shell is the interface for interacting with the system through commands.

flashcards.q: What is Swap used for?
flashcards.a: It uses part of the storage as additional memory when needed.

flashcards.q: What do the `$` and `#` prompt symbols indicate?
flashcards.a: `$` indicates a regular user, and `#` indicates a superuser.

flashcards.q: What is the basic command syntax in Linux, and can options be combined?
flashcards.a: `command option argument`, with spaces required between each part. Options can be combined, e.g. `ls -ld` is equivalent to `ls -l -d`.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `cd`, `cd ~`, `cd $HOME`, and `cd -`?
flashcards.a: `cd`, `cd ~`, and `cd $HOME` all go to the home directory; `cd -` goes back to the previous directory.

flashcards.q: What does `ls -ltr` do compared to `ls -lt`?
flashcards.a: `ls -lt` sorts by time; `ls -ltr` sorts by time in reverse order.

flashcards.q: How are hidden files identified in Linux?
flashcards.a: Files and directories starting with `.` are hidden.

flashcards.q: What does the wildcard pattern `[!a-c]*` match?
flashcards.a: Files that do not start with `a`, `b`, or `c`.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `head -n N file` and `tail -n N file`?
flashcards.a: `head -n N file` shows the first N lines of a file, while `tail -n N file` shows the last N lines.

flashcards.q: What do the `-r`/`-R` and `-f` options mean when used with commands like `cp` or `rm`?
flashcards.a: `-r`/`-R` means recursive (applies to directories and their contents), and `-f` means force (skips confirmation).

flashcards.q: What does `grep -B 2 hager dir` do?
flashcards.a: Shows the match for "hager" along with the 2 lines before each match.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `grep -i` and `grep -l`?
flashcards.a: `grep -i` makes the search case-insensitive; `grep -l` shows only the names of files containing the pattern, not the matching lines.

flashcards.q: What is an inode, and how does it relate to hard links?
flashcards.a: An inode is allocated to every file or directory to store its metadata/data location. A hard link refers to the same inode as the original file — they share the same data.

flashcards.q: Can a hard link point to a directory?
flashcards.a: No, a hard link cannot link directories.

flashcards.q: When does the data of a hard-linked file actually get deleted?
flashcards.a: The data remains as long as at least one hard link to it still exists.

flashcards.q: What does a soft link point to, as opposed to a hard link?
flashcards.a: A soft link points to a path, whereas a hard link points to the same inode/data as the original.

flashcards.q: Is `/root` the same as `/home/root`?
flashcards.a: No — `/root` is the home directory of the superuser, and it is explicitly not the same as `/home/root`.

flashcards.q: What is the purpose of `/etc` and `/var`?
flashcards.a: `/etc` holds configuration files; `/var` holds variable data, such as `/var/tmp`.

flashcards.q: What do `Ctrl+K` and `Ctrl+U` do in the terminal?
flashcards.a: `Ctrl+K` cuts from the cursor to the end of the line; `Ctrl+U` cuts from the cursor to the beginning of the line.

flashcards.q: Why do man pages have numbered sections, and what do sections 1, 5, and 8 document?
flashcards.a: Because some words (like "passwd") refer to more than one thing. Section 1 documents executable programs/user commands, section 5 documents file formats and configuration file structure, and section 8 documents system administration commands (root-level).

flashcards.q: What does `man passwd` show by default if you don't specify a section number?
flashcards.a: It shows the lowest-numbered match it finds, usually the command page (section 1).

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `man`, `whatis`, and `command --help`?
flashcards.a: `man command` gives full details, `whatis command` gives a one-line description, and `command --help` prints a condensed list of that command's available options.

flashcards.q: What does `man -k "keyword"` do, and what does it rely on behind the scenes?
flashcards.a: It searches the short description line of every installed man page for the keyword and lists matching commands. It relies on the `mandb` search database, which may need to be built with `mandb` on a fresh system.

flashcards.q: What does `whereis useradd` tell you?
flashcards.a: Whether the command exists on the machine and where its files are stored (binary, man page, and sometimes source files).

flashcards.q: What are the three data channels (streams) every Linux command is connected to, and their File Descriptor numbers?
flashcards.a: Standard Input (stdin, FD 0), Standard Output (stdout, FD 1), and Standard Error (stderr, FD 2).

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `>` and `>>`?
flashcards.a: `>` overwrites the target file's contents completely with no warning; `>>` appends new output to the end of the file without touching existing content.

flashcards.q: What does `find / -name passwd 2> /dev/null` do?
flashcards.a: It searches the entire filesystem for "passwd" and discards only the error messages (like "Permission denied") by sending them to `/dev/null`, while successful results still print normally to the screen.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `&>` and `2>&1`?
flashcards.a: `&>` is a modern shorthand that sends both stdout and stderr into one file in a single symbol. `2>&1` is the traditional method that must come after a `>` redirection and works by pointing stderr (Channel 2) to wherever stdout (Channel 1) is already going.

flashcards.q: What does the pipeline `ls -l | grep ^-` do?
flashcards.a: It lists files in long format, then filters to show only lines starting with `-`, which represents regular files (as opposed to `d` for directories or `l` for symbolic links).

flashcards.q: What three things does `wc` count, and in what order does it print them?
flashcards.a: Lines, words, and characters, always in that order.

flashcards.q: What does `ls -R /etc | wc -l` tell you?
flashcards.a: The total number of files and folders inside `/etc` and all its subfolders combined, since `-R` makes the listing recursive and `wc -l` counts the resulting lines.

flashcards.q: What are the four main modes in vim, and how do you enter each?
flashcards.a: Normal mode (default, entered by pressing `Esc`), Insert mode (press `i` from Normal mode), Visual mode (press `v` from Normal mode), and Command mode (press `:` from Normal mode).

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `:wq` and `:q!` in vim?
flashcards.a: `:wq` saves your changes and quits; `:q!` quits without saving, discarding all changes made since opening the file.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between a shell variable and a user-defined variable in Bash?
flashcards.a: Shell variables (like `$PATH`, `$HOME`, `$USER`) are built into Bash automatically for configuration purposes. User-defined variables are ones you create yourself to temporarily store values during your session.

flashcards.q: What does `export` do to a variable, and what happens without it?
flashcards.a: `export` makes a variable visible to any sub-shell opened afterward, with the same name and value. Without `export`, the variable stays trapped only in the current shell and sub-shells have no knowledge of it.

flashcards.q: What are the three UID categories in Linux, and their ranges?
flashcards.a: Super user (root) is UID 0; system users are UID 1–999 (1–200 statically reserved, 201–999 dynamically assigned); regular users are UID 1000 and above.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `su - username` and `su username`?
flashcards.a: `su - username` fully loads that user's environment as if they logged in directly (home directory, shell config, PATH, last-login display). `su username` is a lighter switch that keeps your own current environment and directory.

flashcards.q: Why should you use `visudo` instead of editing `/etc/sudoers` directly with vim?
flashcards.a: `visudo` opens the file in a protected session that checks syntax for errors before saving, refusing to save a broken version. Editing directly with vim risks a typo silently breaking the entire permissions system and locking out all administrators.

flashcards.q: What does `find / -name <option>` do?
flashcards.a: Searches the entire system starting from root for files matching the given name.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between FD1 and FD2?
flashcards.a: FD1 is standard output (std output), and FD2 is standard error (std Error).

flashcards.q: How do you redirect only the error output of a command, and how do you get both output and error separately?
flashcards.a: Use `2>` to redirect only the error stream; without specifying, a command's normal output goes to std output and only one stream is captured unless you redirect explicitly (e.g. `2>` for errors).

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `>` and `>>`?
flashcards.a: `>` overrides the destination file's contents, while `>>` appends to it instead of overwriting.

flashcards.q: What is `/dev/null`?
flashcards.a: A special virtual device file that acts like a black hole for data — anything written to it disappears.

flashcards.q: What are the main manual page sections mentioned?
flashcards.a: Section 1 is User Commands (regular page), Section 5 is Configuration files, and Section 8 is System Administrator commands.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `man -k passwd` and `man -w passwd`?
flashcards.a: `man -k passwd` searches man page descriptions for "passwd" as a keyword, while `man -w passwd` shows the location/path of the passwd man page.

flashcards.q: What does `Command --help` return compared to `man Command`?
flashcards.a: `--help` returns only the options for the command, while `man` acts as full documentation/description.

flashcards.q: What are the four Vim modes?
flashcards.a: Command Mode (default), Insert Mode (update), Visual Mode (select), and Ex/Command Line Mode.

flashcards.q: How do you enter Insert Mode in Vim, and how do you exit any mode?
flashcards.a: Press `i` to enter Insert Mode; press `ESC` to exit back to Command Mode.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `:w`, `:wq`, `:q!`, and `:q`?
flashcards.a: `:w` saves and keeps the file open, `:wq` saves and quits, `:q!` quits without saving, and `:q` quits only if there are no unsaved changes (otherwise it prompts).

flashcards.q: What do `dd`, `yy`/`gy`, `p`, and `u` do in Vim?
flashcards.a: `dd` cuts/deletes a line, `yy` or `gy` copies a line, `p` pastes, and `u` undoes the last action.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between `v`, `Shift+V`, and `Ctrl+v` in Vim's visual modes?
flashcards.a: `v` enters character-wise Visual Mode, `Shift+V` selects entire lines, and `Ctrl+v` selects a block/column *(لعمود)*.

flashcards.q: What does the Vim command `:%s/login/nologin/g` do?
flashcards.a: It performs a global find-and-replace across the file, replacing every occurrence of "login" with "nologin".

flashcards.q: What does `:.! date` do in Vim?
flashcards.a: It runs the external `date` command and inserts its output, then returns to the same place in the file *(خارج ولكن يعود للمكان مره ثانيه)*.

flashcards.q: What is a pipeline in Bash, and what does `ls -l | grep ^-` do?
flashcards.a: A pipeline passes the output of one command as input to another command. `ls -l | grep ^-` filters the long listing to show only regular files (lines starting with `-`).

flashcards.q: What do `wc -l`, `wc -w`, and `wc -c` count?
flashcards.a: `wc -l` counts lines only, `wc -w` counts words only, and `wc -c` counts characters only.

flashcards.q: What does the search pattern `\<th` match?
flashcards.a: Any word containing "th" (word-boundary search for "th").

flashcards.q: What does `whereis Command` do?
flashcards.a: Shows where a command's binary, source, and man page files are located.

flashcards.q: What does `ls -li` add vs `ls -l`, and why use `stat file`?
flashcards.a: `ls -li` shows inode numbers (first column) via `l`+`i`; `stat file` shows inode, size, blocks, and all three timestamps (Access/Modify/Change) plus `df -i` for inode exhaustion.

flashcards.q: Why does `rm -- -f` use `--` and what does `touch "my file"` fix?
flashcards.a: `--` ends option parsing so `-f` is treated as filename, not flag. Spaces split arguments — quote `"my file"` or escape `my\ file` to keep it one name.

flashcards.q: When does `df -h` lie and `df -i` matter? Give an example.
flashcards.a: `df -h` shows bytes; `df -i` shows inodes. A disk can be “No space left” with free GB if inodes are 100% — check `df -i` and `du --maxdepth=1` vs `ncdu` for hogs.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between `cp -r` and `cp -a`, and when to use `mv -i`?
flashcards.a: `cp -a` = archive (preserves perms/symlinks/xattrs) better than `-r` for backups. `mv -i` prompts before silently overwriting the destination.

flashcards.q: Explain `> file 2>&1` order vs `&> file` and `PIPESTATUS`.
flashcards.a: `> file 2>&1` must have `2>&1` last — it points stderr to where stdout now goes. `&> file` is shorthand for the same. `echo ${PIPESTATUS[@]}` shows each pipe stage exit code, not just last.

flashcards.q: Why does `man -k` sometimes return nothing and how to fix?
flashcards.a: `man -k` searches the `mandb` index. On fresh/minimal systems the DB may be empty — run `sudo mandb` once to build it, then `apropos`/`man -k` works.

flashcards.q: In vim, what does `:%s/old/new/gc` do and how to recover from a swap file?
flashcards.a: `%` whole file, `s` substitute, `g` global, `c` confirm each. If vim warns about `.swp`, check `ls -la .*.swp` and recover with `vim -r file` then `rm .file.swp` after.

flashcards.q: Why is `sudo visudo` safer than `vim /etc/sudoers` and how to check syntax without editing?
flashcards.a: `visudo` locks and syntax-checks before saving — a typo with plain `vim` can lock all sudo. Check without editing via `sudo visudo -c` and view filtered rules with `grep -vE '^[[:space:]]*(#|$)' /etc/sudoers`.

flashcards.q: What does `chmod 644` mean and how does `umask 022` affect new files?
flashcards.a: `644` = `rw-r--r--` (owner rw, group r, other r). `umask 022` subtracts `w` for group/other, so `touch` creates `644` and `mkdir` `755`. Never `777` on web roots.

flashcards.q: How does `grep -F` differ from `grep -E` and which is faster?
flashcards.a: `grep -F` treats pattern as fixed string (no regex) and is ~10× faster; use `-F` for literals like `error.log`. `grep -E` enables extended regex (`^`, `+`, `|`).
